en.title: Master of Public Health (MPH): the whole course
en.short: How the MPH is organised, what it covers and how to study it well.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text: These notes teach public health concepts to master’s students. They are not medical advice and do not replace your teachers, textbooks, local protocols or official guidance. They give no drug doses. Clinical and public health guidelines change and differ between countries, so check the current national ministry of health or World Health Organization (WHO) source before applying anything. Public health decisions affect whole populations, so accuracy, ethics and local context matter.

sections.heading: What public health is
sections.text: Public health is the organised effort to prevent disease, prolong life and promote health across populations. It asks who is affected, why, and what can be done. Its core functions are often described as assessment of health needs, policy development, and assurance of services. Prevention may be primary, before disease starts; secondary, finding disease early; or tertiary, reducing complications. It draws on epidemiology, biostatistics, social sciences, economics, management, law and ethics. Clinical care treats individuals; public health works on the conditions that shape health for everyone, including water, housing, food, work and health services.

sections.heading: How the programme is organised
sections.text: An MPH is a master’s degree. It assumes a first degree, sometimes in another field, and starts each topic from its foundations. Length and award differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, an MPH is commonly one to two years full-time, and part-time routes take longer; some schools require a health-related first degree or relevant experience. In the United Kingdom, one year full-time is common; in the United States, two years full-time is common. Awards may be MPH, MSc or MPhil in public health; titles vary. Most programmes combine taught modules, assignments, examinations and a supervised dissertation or project. Check your own handbook for modules, credit rules, fees and dissertation requirements.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text: Teaching usually begins with foundations: concepts, history and functions; determinants and equity; social and behavioural foundations. The quantitative core follows: epidemiology measures; study designs and causal inference; descriptive biostatistics; estimation and hypothesis testing; regression. Research skills come next: methods and protocols; ethics and governance; systematic reviews and meta-analysis. Policy and practice then follow: public health ethics and law; policy, systems and management; economics and financing; programme planning and evaluation; implementation science and scale-up; health promotion. Applied fields include environmental health and sanitation; occupational health and safety; communicable disease control; noncommunicable diseases; maternal, newborn and child health; nutrition; global health; health informatics; emergency preparedness; quality improvement and patient safety. Cross-cutting themes include equity, ethics, evidence use, community participation and One Health, which links human, animal and environmental health.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text: Study for understanding, not recall alone. For each topic, ask what problem it addresses, what data it uses, what it can and cannot show, and how it guides action. Work through calculations by hand, then check with software. Read one good textbook chapter and one recent review. Practise critical appraisal, protocol writing and clear reporting. Use local examples, such as a malaria outbreak or a city water supply, to connect theory to practice. Space revision over weeks and test yourself. Keep a notebook of definitions and formulas. Learn to explain measures such as incidence and prevalence in plain words. When reading a paper, write its question, design, main result and limitation in four lines. Discuss ethical and political choices with classmates, and note where reasonable people disagree.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Common mistakes include memorising definitions without applying them, confusing association with causation, and treating a p-value as proof of importance. Students also ignore equity and local context, quote one country’s guideline as universal, and skip ethics or governance. Weak referencing and plagiarism are serious. Another mistake is studying only for examinations and never practising protocol writing, data analysis or evaluation. In group work, agree roles and cite every source. If a calculation or result looks odd, check units, denominators and missing data before interpreting it. Check your handbook and ask supervisors early.

keyPoints: Public health works on populations, prevention and the conditions that shape health.
An MPH assumes a first degree and builds from foundations to master’s depth.
Length, award and entry rules differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Epidemiology, biostatistics and research methods form the quantitative core.
Study for understanding and practise calculation, appraisal and writing.
These notes teach concepts and are not medical advice or official guidance.

en.title: Public health: concepts, history and functions
en.short: This summary covers definitions, core functions, population versus clinical care, history and organisation.

sections.heading: What public health is
sections.text:
Public health is the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life and improving health through organised efforts of society. Its scope includes infectious disease control and the wider conditions that shape health, such as water, sanitation, nutrition and housing. It studies populations, not only patients.

Population health means the health outcomes of a defined group. Clinical care diagnoses and treats an individual. Public health asks why the group became ill and what can change for everyone. In a town with many childhood diarrhoea cases, clinical care treats each child; public health checks water and sanitation, finds a shared cause, and works with the water authority and schools to prevent cases.

sections.heading: Core functions and services
sections.text:
Common frameworks describe three core functions. Assessment means measuring and monitoring health needs and risks. Policy development means using evidence, law and partnership to decide what to do. Assurance means ensuring services are delivered, regulated and accessible, and that people are linked to care.

Essential public health services are detailed lists built on these functions. The United States uses the ten Essential Public Health Services. WHO and several regions use Essential Public Health Functions. The lists differ but usually cover surveillance (ongoing tracking of disease and risk factors), health protection (control of infections and environmental hazards), promotion, prevention, workforce, governance and emergency response. They are planning tools, not law.

sections.heading: History and organisation
sections.text:
Public health grew from sanitary reform, vaccination and epidemiology. John Snow linked cholera in London in 1854 to a contaminated water pump. The Public Health Act 1848 in England and Wales set up a General Board of Health and allowed local boards of health. Later milestones include germ theory, WHO in 1948, and the Alma-Ata Declaration on primary health care in 1978. Its roots are multidisciplinary: epidemiology, biostatistics, clinical medicine, social sciences, environmental health, economics, management, law and ethics.

Countries organise public health differently. Some are centralised, some decentralised, and many are mixed. In Nigeria, federal, state and local governments share duties with the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention. Laws and structures change; check current official sources.

keyPoints: Public health works through organised action on populations, not only individual patients.
Population health describes the health outcomes of a defined group; clinical care treats individuals.
The three core functions are assessment, policy development and assurance.
Essential public health services are detailed planning lists that vary between countries and frameworks.
John Snow’s 1854 cholera investigation and the 1848 Public Health Act in England and Wales are key historical markers.
Public health is multidisciplinary, and its organisation differs between centralised, decentralised and mixed systems, so check current national sources.

en.title: Determinants of health and health equity
en.short: How social, economic, environmental, behavioural and biological factors shape health, and how inequities are measured.

sections.heading: Determinants
sections.text: Determinants of health are the conditions and factors that influence health across life. Social determinants include education, social support, culture and gender norms. Economic determinants include income, employment and wealth. Environmental determinants include water, sanitation, air quality, housing and climate. Behavioural determinants include smoking, diet, physical activity and alcohol use. Biological determinants include age, sex, genes and immune status. These factors interact: low income may limit housing quality, which affects respiratory health, while stress and poor diet add risk. They operate at individual, community and societal levels.

sections.heading: Inequality and frameworks
sections.text: A health inequality is any observed difference in health between groups. A health inequity is a difference that is avoidable, unfair and unjust. Not every inequality is an inequity: a height difference between older men and younger women may reflect biology or age. A gap in child vaccination between rich and poor districts is usually an inequity because it is avoidable and rooted in unequal access. Frameworks organise determinants. The Dahlgren and Whitehead rainbow model places the individual at the centre, surrounded by social and community networks, living and working conditions, and general socioeconomic, cultural and environmental conditions. The WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health framework separates structural determinants, such as governance, policies and socioeconomic position, from intermediary determinants, such as material circumstances, psychosocial factors, behaviour, biology and the health system. Frameworks help planners see where to act.

sections.heading: Measuring and prioritising
sections.text: Measure inequities by comparing rates. Example: District A has 200 cases in 10,000 people (2.0%); District B has 100 in 10,000 (1.0%). Absolute difference = 2.0% − 1.0% = 1.0 percentage point. Relative difference = 2.0 ÷ 1.0 = 2.0, so District A has twice the rate. If District A is poorer and the gap is avoidable, it is an inequity. The concentration index summarises inequality across socioeconomic rank. Prioritise by burden, severity, trend, avoidability, equity impact, feasibility and community priorities. Policy responses vary by country; check current national and WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Determinants of health include social, economic, environmental, behavioural and biological factors that interact across life.
A health inequality is any observed difference; a health inequity is a difference that is avoidable, unfair and unjust.
The Dahlgren and Whitehead model and the WHO CSDH framework organise determinants into layers or structural and intermediary factors.
Absolute gap = rate in group A − rate in group B; relative gap = rate in group A ÷ rate in group B.
Prioritise inequities by burden, severity, trend, avoidability, equity impact, feasibility and community priorities.
Policy responses vary by country, so check current national and WHO guidance.

en.title: Social and behavioural foundations of public health
en.short: Theories, culture, networks, stigma, community participation and qualitative views of health.

sections.heading: Theories
sections.text: Social and behavioural theories explain why people and groups act as they do. The health belief model says action depends on perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits and barriers, plus cues and self-efficacy. Social cognitive theory stresses reciprocal determinism: person, behaviour and environment affect one another, and self-efficacy, the belief in one’s ability, predicts action. The theory of planned behaviour links attitudes, subjective norms and perceived behavioural control to intention. The socio-ecological model places behaviour within individual, interpersonal, community, organisational and policy levels. Diffusion of innovations describes how new practices spread through networks over time.

sections.heading: Culture and networks
sections.text: Culture is shared learned beliefs, values and customs. It shapes what counts as illness, who is consulted and what food or care is acceptable. Social networks are the ties between people; they transmit norms, support and information. A mother in a Nigerian town may delay seeking care for a child’s fever because her neighbours say it is ordinary malaria and a church group advises prayer first. The network is not simply a barrier: respected community members can also speed referral.

sections.heading: Stigma and illness
sections.text: Stigma is a mark of social disgrace that excludes people. It can delay diagnosis and treatment, as with HIV or mental illness. Illness behaviour is how people notice, interpret and act on symptoms. It depends on culture, previous experience, gender, cost and trust in services. Labelling theory notes that labels can become self-fulfilling. These ideas explain practices; they inform health promotion but do not replace its intervention design.

sections.heading: Community and qualitative
sections.text: Community participation means involving residents in defining problems, planning and carrying out action. It improves fit and trust, though it takes time and can favour louder voices. Qualitative methods such as interviews and focus groups explore meanings, experiences and social context. They answer why and how, not how many. Together these perspectives help public health explain behaviour and design acceptable, ethical action.

keyPoints: Social and behavioural theories explain health practices at individual, interpersonal and community levels.
The health belief model uses perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers, cues and self-efficacy.
Social cognitive theory emphasises reciprocal determinism and self-efficacy.
Culture and social networks shape symptom interpretation, norms and care-seeking.
Stigma and labelling can delay diagnosis and exclude people.
Community participation and qualitative methods improve fit, trust and understanding of meaning.

en.title: Epidemiology: measures of disease frequency and association
en.short: Incidence, prevalence, risk and odds ratios, standardisation, and interpreting association and impact.

sections.heading: Frequency measures
sections.text: Incidence is the number of new cases in a population at risk during a stated period. Incidence proportion, or risk, is new cases divided by people at risk at the start: risk = new cases ÷ population at risk. It ranges from 0 to 1. Incidence rate uses person-time: rate = new cases ÷ total person-time at risk, so it can exceed 1 per person-year. Prevalence is all existing cases divided by the population: prevalence = cases ÷ population. It reflects both incidence and duration. A long disease raises prevalence even when incidence is low.

sections.heading: Association measures
sections.text: Risk ratio compares risks: RR = risk exposed ÷ risk unexposed. Odds ratio compares odds: OR = (a ÷ b) ÷ (c ÷ d), where a and c are cases and b and d non-cases in exposed and unexposed groups. For rare outcomes OR approximates RR; for common outcomes it is further from 1. Example: in a cohort, 20 of 100 exposed and 10 of 100 unexposed develop disease. Risk exposed = 20 ÷ 100 = 0.20; risk unexposed = 10 ÷ 100 = 0.10; RR = 0.20 ÷ 0.10 = 2.0. Odds exposed = 20 ÷ 80 = 0.25; odds unexposed = 10 ÷ 90 = 0.111; OR = 0.25 ÷ 0.111 = 2.25. The exposed group has twice the risk.

sections.heading: Standardisation and pitfalls
sections.text: Crude rates can mislead when age structures differ. Direct standardisation applies study age-specific rates to a standard population. Indirect standardisation compares observed cases with expected cases from standard rates. Association measures such as the risk ratio describe relative differences; impact measures such as the risk difference describe absolute effects. Risk difference = risk exposed − risk unexposed; attributable fraction among exposed = (RR − 1) ÷ RR. A common pitfall is reading prevalence as incidence: prevalence includes old and new cases and depends on survival and recovery. Another is calling any ratio a risk ratio when the data came from a case-control study, which compares cases with controls rather than following a population at risk, so the odds ratio is the usual measure.

keyPoints: Incidence counts new cases in people at risk; prevalence counts all existing cases.
Risk = new cases ÷ people at risk at start; incidence rate = new cases ÷ person-time.
Risk ratio = risk exposed ÷ risk unexposed; odds ratio = (a ÷ b) ÷ (c ÷ d).
Risk difference = risk exposed − risk unexposed; attributable fraction among exposed = (RR − 1) ÷ RR.
Direct standardisation applies study rates to a standard population; indirect standardisation compares observed with expected cases.
Prevalence depends on incidence and duration, so it must not be read as incidence.

en.title: Epidemiologic study designs and causal inference
en.short: How cross-sectional, case-control, cohort, ecological and randomised designs support causal inference.

sections.heading: Designs and questions
sections.text:
Design choice follows the research question. Cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome at one time; they estimate prevalence and generate hypotheses but cannot show temporality. Case-control studies start with cases (people with the outcome) and controls (comparable people without it), then look back at exposure. They suit rare outcomes but risk recall bias.

Cohort studies follow exposed and unexposed people forward and measure incident outcomes; they establish that exposure preceded outcome but are slower and costly for rare outcomes. Ecological studies compare groups such as districts, not individuals; they are cheap for monitoring but risk ecological fallacy, where a group-level association is wrongly read as an individual one. Randomised trials allocate interventions by chance, balancing known and unknown confounders; they give the strongest evidence for an intervention’s causal effect but may be impractical or unethical for harmful exposures.

sections.heading: Bias and modification
sections.text:
Bias is systematic error distorting association. Selection bias occurs when studied people differ from the target population in ways linked to exposure and outcome, such as volunteers or loss to follow-up. Information bias comes from wrong measurement, such as different recall between cases and controls.

Confounding occurs when a third factor is associated with exposure and independently affects outcome, creating a non-causal association; randomisation and adjustment reduce it. Effect modification is different: the exposure-outcome association changes across levels of another factor, such as age or sex. It is a finding to report, not a nuisance to remove.

sections.heading: Causal inference
sections.text:
Causal inference asks whether an association is likely causal. Bradford Hill viewpoints include temporality, strength, consistency, plausibility, dose-response and experiment; temporality is essential, but no single viewpoint proves causation.

Example: a cohort follows 200 exposed and 200 unexposed people; asthma occurs in 20 and 10. Risk is 20/200 = 10% exposed and 10/200 = 5% unexposed, so risk ratio = 10% ÷ 5% = 2.0. This suggests doubled risk, but confounding, selection and measurement error must be assessed before calling it causal.

keyPoints: The research question determines the design; no design is best for every question.
Cross-sectional studies measure prevalence but cannot establish temporality.
Case-control studies suit rare outcomes; cohort studies measure incidence and can show exposure preceded outcome.
Ecological studies compare groups and risk ecological fallacy; randomised trials balance confounders and best test interventions.
Selection, information and confounding bias distort associations; effect modification is a real difference across strata.
Causal inference uses Bradford Hill viewpoints, especially temporality; risk ratio = risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed.

en.title: Biostatistics: data, probability and descriptive analysis
en.short: Health data types, sampling variation, distributions, descriptive statistics, rates and honest graphs.

sections.heading: Data types
sections.text: Health data are observations about people, places or services. They may be categorical (groups such as sex or disease present/absent) or numerical (counts, ages, blood pressure). Numerical data may be discrete (whole counts) or continuous (any value on a scale). Data also have a level of measurement: nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio. Knowing the type matters because it decides which summary and graph are valid. A mean of nominal labels is meaningless.

sections.heading: Variation and distributions
sections.text: Sampling variation is the natural difference between samples from the same population. A sample estimate is therefore not the population value. Probability distributions describe how values are expected to occur. The binomial distribution models the number of events in a fixed number of trials with the same probability, such as cases in a group. The Poisson distribution models counts in time or space when events are rare. The normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped; many continuous measurements are roughly normal. Distributions guide summaries and later inference.

sections.heading: Describing data
sections.text: Descriptive statistics summarise a sample. For categorical data use counts and proportions. For numerical data report centre and spread: mean and standard deviation for roughly symmetric data; median and interquartile range for skewed data. The mean is Σx/n. The median is the middle value. The interquartile range is the spread of the middle half of values, from the first to the third quartile. Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean. Always report the number of observations and missing values. Example ages 24, 28, 30, 35, 41: sum 158, mean 31.6 years, median 30 years, range 17 years.

sections.heading: Rates and graphs
sections.text: A rate expresses events per population at risk per unit time. For example, 8 new cases in 20,000 people over one year (20,000 person-years) give 8 ÷ 20,000 × 1,000 = 0.4 cases per 1,000 person-years. Graphs should have labelled axes, units, a clear title and a stated denominator. Bar charts suit categories; histograms suit continuous data; line graphs suit time trends. Misleading graph practices include truncated axes, changing denominators, cherry-picked time periods and confusing counts with rates.

keyPoints: Categorical data need counts and proportions; numerical data need a measure of centre and spread.
Sampling variation means a sample estimate differs from the population value.
The mean is Σx/n; the median is the middle value and is better for skewed data.
Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean; interquartile range describes the middle half.
A rate is events divided by population at risk, multiplied by a stated base and time unit.
Check axes, denominators, missing data and whether counts or rates are shown before trusting a graph or summary.

en.title: Biostatistics: estimation and hypothesis testing
en.short: This summary covers sampling distributions, confidence intervals, p values, errors and common tests, with interpretation.

sections.heading: Estimation and intervals
sections.text: Estimation uses a sample to infer a population value. A statistic such as a mean varies between samples; its sampling distribution describes that variation. The standard error (SE) is the standard deviation of this distribution and shrinks as sample size grows. A 95% confidence interval is often estimate ± 1.96 × SE. If mean systolic blood pressure is 140 mmHg with SE 2 mmHg, the interval is 136.08 to 143.92 mmHg. Across repeated samples, about 95% of intervals built this way contain the true mean. It is not a 95% probability that this interval contains the truth.

sections.heading: Testing and errors
sections.text: A hypothesis test compares a null hypothesis, usually no difference, with an alternative. The p value is the probability of data as extreme as, or more extreme than, the observed data if the null is true. It is not the probability that the null is true. Type I error is rejecting a true null, a false positive, with probability alpha, often 0.05. Type II error is failing to reject a false null, a false negative, with probability beta. Power is 1 − beta, the chance of detecting a real effect.

sections.heading: Tests and interpretation
sections.text: Common tests include the t test, chi-square test and analysis of variance (ANOVA). A t test compares one mean with a value, paired measurements, or two group means. A chi-square test assesses association between two categorical variables. ANOVA compares means across three or more groups. These tests have assumptions, such as approximate normality for t tests and ANOVA, and adequate expected counts for chi-square. Statistical significance is not public health significance. A huge study can give a tiny p value for a trivial difference, such as a 1 mmHg blood pressure fall. Judge importance by effect size, confidence interval, population impact, cost and equity.

keyPoints: A 95% confidence interval is often estimate ± 1.96 × SE; it estimates a range that would contain the true value in about 95% of repeated samples.
The p value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis is true, not the probability that the null is true.
Type I error is a false positive (probability alpha); Type II error is a false negative (probability beta); power is 1 − beta.
The t statistic is t = (estimate − hypothesised value) ÷ SE; t tests compare means, chi-square tests test association between categorical variables, and ANOVA compares three or more means.
Check test assumptions: approximate normality for t tests and ANOVA, and adequate expected counts for chi-square.
Statistical significance is not public health significance; report effect size and confidence interval, and judge importance by population impact, cost and equity.

en.title: Biostatistics: regression models for health data
en.short: Linear, logistic, Poisson and survival models; confounding, assumptions and reading adjusted effects.

sections.heading: Why regression
sections.text: Regression models describe how an outcome changes with one or more explanatory variables. They estimate an effect while holding other variables constant, test whether the effect is likely due to chance, and allow prediction. In health data the outcome may be continuous, binary, a count or a time to an event. The model must match the outcome type.

sections.heading: Four model types
sections.text: Linear regression is for a continuous outcome, such as blood pressure. Its coefficient is the mean change in the outcome per one-unit rise in exposure, with other terms fixed. Logistic regression is for a binary outcome, such as anaemia yes or no. It models log odds; exponentiating a coefficient gives an odds ratio. Poisson regression is for counts or rates, such as clinic visits per person-year; exponentiating gives a rate ratio. Survival models, such as Cox regression, analyse time to an event when some people are censored, meaning their event time is unknown because follow-up ended. Cox gives a hazard ratio.

sections.heading: Confounding and assumptions
sections.text: A confounder is linked to both exposure and outcome, is not on the causal pathway between them, and distorts their apparent relation. Adjustment means including it in the model, or using design methods such as matching. An adjusted effect compares people with the same confounder values, so it differs from a crude effect. Assumptions differ. Linear models assume a straight-line relation and roughly constant variance. Logistic models assume independent observations and linearity on the log-odds scale. Poisson models assume independent counts and variance close to the mean. Cox models assume proportional hazards: the hazard ratio stays constant over time. Check assumptions with plots and sensitivity analyses.

sections.heading: Reading results
sections.text: Suppose a logistic model of anaemia on malaria, adjusted for age, gives malaria coefficient 0.693. exp(0.693) = 2.0. Adjusted odds ratio is 2.0: at the same age, parasitaemic children have twice the odds of anaemia. A 95% confidence interval including 1.0 suggests no clear adjusted association. Report the effect, interval and adjusted variables.

keyPoints: Match the model to the outcome: linear for continuous, logistic for binary, Poisson for counts or rates, and Cox for time to event.
In linear regression the coefficient is the mean change in outcome per one-unit exposure, with other variables fixed.
In logistic regression exp(coefficient) is an odds ratio; in Poisson regression exp(coefficient) is a rate ratio; in Cox regression exp(coefficient) is a hazard ratio.
Adjustment for a confounder compares people with the same confounder values and gives an adjusted effect.
Check assumptions: linearity, independence, variance structure and proportional hazards.
Report adjusted effects with confidence intervals and state which variables were adjusted for.

en.title: Research methods and study protocols
en.short: Forming questions, choosing designs, sampling, measurement, data management and writing a protocol.

sections.heading: Question and design
sections.text: Start with a research question that names the population, exposure or intervention, comparison where relevant, outcome, time and setting. A vague question produces vague methods. The design must answer that question and be feasible. A cross-sectional survey measures exposure and outcome at one time; it is quick but cannot establish order. A cohort follows people over time and can show temporality, but costs more and loses people to follow-up. Choose the simplest design that protects validity, meaning the results are trustworthy and not distorted by bias. Feasibility covers time, money, staff, access and skills. Ethical review asks whether the benefit justifies any burden or risk.

sections.heading: Sampling and measurement
sections.text: Sampling is selecting participants from a defined population. Probability methods, such as simple random or cluster sampling, give every eligible person a known chance of selection and reduce selection bias. Non-probability methods, such as convenience sampling, are faster but limit generalisability. The sampling frame, the list from which the sample is drawn, must match the population; clinic registers, for example, miss people who never attend. Measurement turns concepts into variables. Use validated instruments where they exist, train data collectors, pilot the tools and check reliability. For example, a study of missed antenatal appointments may survey women in one district. A register-based sample misses women who never attended, threatening external validity, that is, generalisability. A pilot can reveal unclear questions and reduce measurement error.

sections.heading: Data and protocol
sections.text: Data management begins before collection: unique identifiers, a codebook that defines each variable, secure storage, controlled access, backups and an audit trail that records changes to the data. Plan cleaning and analysis in advance to avoid selective reporting. The protocol, also called the proposal, is the written plan and the basis for ethical and scientific review. It usually states background, question and objectives, design, setting, participants, sampling, variables and measurement, data management and analysis, ethical considerations, timeline, budget and dissemination. Obtain ethical approval before recruitment, use informed consent, protect confidentiality and follow local data protection rules. Reviewers judge validity, feasibility and ethics together.

keyPoints: A good research question names population, exposure or intervention, comparison, outcome, time and setting.
Choose the simplest design that answers the question while protecting validity and remaining feasible.
Probability sampling reduces selection bias; the sampling frame must cover the population.
Measurement needs validated tools, training and piloting to reduce error.
Plan data management before collection: identifiers, codebook, secure storage, backups and audit trail.
The protocol is the written plan for scientific and ethical review; obtain approval before recruitment.

en.title: Research ethics and governance
en.short: Principles, consent, confidentiality, vulnerability, ethics review, misconduct and data protection.

sections.heading: Principles and consent
sections.text: Research ethics protects participants, communities and public trust. Core principles are respect for persons, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice. Respect for persons means people choose freely and are protected if they cannot. Beneficence means likely benefits outweigh risks; non-maleficence means minimise harm. Justice means fair selection and fair sharing of benefits and burdens. Informed consent has three parts: adequate information, understanding and voluntary choice. Use plain language, disclose purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, alternatives, confidentiality and the right to withdraw. Record consent unless a committee approves another method.

sections.heading: Confidentiality and vulnerability
sections.text: Confidentiality is the duty to keep participant information private. Protect data by collecting only what is needed, using codes instead of names, limiting access, and storing paper and electronic records securely. Anonymisation removes identifiers; pseudonymisation replaces them with codes, but re-identification may still be possible. Vulnerability means a higher risk of harm or reduced ability to protect one’s interests. Children, prisoners, people with cognitive impairment, pregnant women and economically disadvantaged groups may need extra safeguards. Vulnerability is not a reason to exclude groups automatically; it calls for justified inclusion and added protection.

sections.heading: Review and governance
sections.text: An ethics committee (institutional review board) reviews protocols before research starts. It checks scientific value, risk, consent, confidentiality, vulnerability and investigator competence. Approval may require amendments and continuing reports. Governance covers laws, institutional policies and data protection. Research misconduct includes fabrication (making up data or results), falsification (changing or omitting data or results) and plagiarism (using others’ work without credit). Undisclosed conflicts and poor records are integrity breaches. Requirements differ by country and institution. The EU General Data Protection Regulation and Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 set rules. Check national law, regulator guidance and institutional policy.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: Case: Amina, an MPH student, plans interviews with women living with HIV about stigma in a Nigerian town. The committee asks for consent in the local language, private interviews without clinic staff present, coded files on encrypted storage, a distress referral plan and community advice. Clinic staff should not recruit, because women may feel obliged. These safeguards protect confidentiality and reduce vulnerability.

keyPoints: Respect for persons, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice guide research.
Informed consent must be informed, voluntary and documented unless a committee approves otherwise.
Protect confidentiality through minimal data, codes, secure storage and limited access.
Vulnerability calls for extra safeguards, not automatic exclusion.
Ethics committee approval is required before research starts, with amendments and continuing reports.
Fabrication, falsification and plagiarism are misconduct; data laws differ by country and institution.

en.title: Systematic reviews and meta-analysis
en.short: Framing, searching, risk of bias, pooling, heterogeneity, publication bias and GRADE certainty.

sections.heading: Framing and selecting
sections.text: A systematic review answers one focused question using explicit, reproducible methods. Frame it with PICO: population, intervention or exposure, comparator and outcome. Write a protocol first and register it, for example on PROSPERO. Search several databases with a librarian, plus trial registers and grey literature. Record the search date and terms. Two reviewers screen titles, abstracts and full texts against preset eligibility criteria, resolving disagreements by discussion or a third reviewer. Extract data into a piloted form: study setting, design, participants, intervention, outcomes and effect estimates. Report the flow of studies using PRISMA.

sections.heading: Risk of bias and synthesis
sections.text: Assess risk of bias with a design-specific tool, such as Cochrane RoB 2 for randomised trials or ROBINS-I for non-randomised studies. Judge selection, measurement, confounding and reporting problems. Meta-analysis is appropriate when studies ask a sufficiently similar question and provide comparable effect estimates, not merely because several studies exist. Pool risk ratios, odds ratios or mean differences using inverse-variance weighting. For a ratio, RR = (a/(a+b)) ÷ (c/(c+d)). Example: two studies each give RR = 2.0 with 95% CI about 1.08 to 3.71; inverse-variance pooling keeps RR = 2.0 and narrows the 95% CI to about 1.29 to 3.09. Use fixed-effect when one true effect is plausible; use random-effects when effects vary.

sections.heading: Heterogeneity and certainty
sections.text: Heterogeneity is real variation beyond chance. Inspect forest plots, then report I² and tau², the variance of the true effects across studies. I² is the percentage of variability due to heterogeneity rather than sampling error; it does not measure clinical importance. Explore heterogeneity with subgroup analysis or meta-regression, but prespecify these. Publication bias arises when studies, typically small ones with null or negative results, are less likely to be published and so go missing. Assess it with a funnel plot and Egger’s test when at least about ten studies are available; asymmetry suggests small-study effects, not proof of bias. GRADE rates certainty as high, moderate, low or very low, downgrading for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias.

keyPoints: Frame the question with PICO and register a protocol before searching.
Search several databases and screen studies in duplicate, reporting flow with PRISMA.
Use RoB 2 for randomised trials and ROBINS-I for non-randomised studies.
Pool only sufficiently similar studies; pooled effect = Σ(w × effect) ÷ Σw, with w = 1/SE².
For a risk ratio, RR = (a/(a+b)) ÷ (c/(c+d)); pooling two studies each with RR 2.0 keeps the pooled RR at 2.0 and narrows the confidence interval.
Report heterogeneity with I² and tau², assess publication bias with funnel plots and Egger’s test, and rate certainty with GRADE.

en.title: Public health ethics and law
en.short: Ethical frameworks, autonomy versus collective welfare, equity, privacy, stigma and public health law powers.

sections.heading: Frameworks
sections.text: Public health ethics asks what health authorities owe to populations and to individuals. Consequentialism judges actions by outcomes, such as deaths averted. Deontology stresses duties and rights, such as not using people merely as means. Principlism uses four principles: respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice. Public health adds solidarity (shared responsibility for health), reciprocity (support owed to people who bear burdens for others) and precaution (acting on serious threats before full proof). These frameworks conflict, so decisions need reasons that can be defended publicly.

sections.heading: Autonomy and welfare
sections.text: Autonomy is a person’s capacity to decide for themselves. Collective welfare is the good of the whole population. Vaccination, isolation and seatbelt laws show the tension: they protect others but limit choice. Ethics does not say the collective always wins. It asks whether a measure is necessary, proportionate, transparent and the least restrictive option. It also asks who bears the burdens. Case: in a Nigerian district, Amina’s market is closed during a cholera outbreak. The benefit is reduced spread; the harms are lost income and stigma. A fair plan explains reasons, uses the least restrictive measures, offers support and provides review.

sections.heading: Equity privacy stigma
sections.text: Equity means fair treatment according to need, not identical treatment. Public health must avoid worsening unfair differences. Privacy is control over personal information; confidentiality is the duty not to disclose it without consent or lawful reason. Stigma is marking a group as discredited, which can drive people away from testing or care. Good programmes collect only needed data, protect it, involve affected communities and use neutral language. They monitor who is missed or harmed.

sections.heading: Law and limits
sections.text: Public health law gives powers such as notification, inspection, isolation, quarantine and closure of premises. These powers vary by country and must be set in law. In England and Wales, the Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984 provides a framework; Scotland and Northern Ireland have separate arrangements. Nigeria’s Quarantine Act gives federal quarantine powers, while states also make health laws. Limits include legality, legitimate aim, necessity, proportionality, due process and review. Courts may check whether powers are used lawfully.

keyPoints: Public health ethics balances consequences, duties, rights and justice.
Autonomy and collective welfare conflict; measures should be necessary, proportionate, transparent and least restrictive.
Equity means fair treatment by need and avoiding unfair differences.
Privacy and confidentiality protect personal data; stigma can deter care.
Public health law powers vary by country and must be lawful, necessary and proportionate.
Courts and review bodies can check whether powers are used lawfully.

en.title: Health policy, systems and management
en.short: Policy process, WHO building blocks, governance, financing, workforce, planning and change.

sections.heading: Policy process
sections.text: Public policy is a course of action chosen by an authority. The policy process usually moves through agenda setting, formulation, adoption, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation, with feedback. Agenda setting decides which problems get attention. Formulation designs options and assesses costs and effects. Adoption gives legal or administrative authority. Implementation depends on organisations, staff and resources. Evaluation asks whether goals were met and for whom. Policy is political as well as technical, so evidence, values and stakeholders all matter.

sections.heading: System building blocks
sections.text: The World Health Organization (WHO) describes six health system building blocks: service delivery; health workforce; health information systems; medical products, vaccines and technologies; financing; and leadership and governance. They are a framework for diagnosis, not a universal model. Countries differ in history, income, law and organisation, so systems differ and a model from one country may not transfer. Governance means stewardship, accountability and regulation. Financing has three functions: collecting revenue, pooling risk, and purchasing services. Workforce covers numbers, skill mix, distribution and motivation. Service delivery concerns access, quality and referral. Medicines need selection, procurement, supply and rational use. Information needs reliable data that managers use.

sections.heading: Planning and change
sections.text: Planning starts with situation analysis, then priorities, targets, costing, implementation and review. Leadership sets direction and builds trust; management organises resources and routines. Organisational behaviour studies how people and groups act in institutions, including motivation, power and culture. Change management plans the transition, communicates reasons, involves staff and monitors effects. Lewin’s unfreeze, change and refreeze is one simple model; no single model fits every setting.

sections.heading: County case
sections.text: Suppose a fictional county in Kenya has long clinic waits. The team maps the building blocks and finds staff absent from rural posts and frequent stock-outs. It plans to redeploy staff, improve stock data and hold monthly reviews. The manager explains the change, trains supervisors and checks waiting times. The team reviews results and adjusts the plan.

keyPoints: The policy process runs from agenda setting through formulation, adoption, implementation and evaluation.
WHO’s six building blocks are service delivery, workforce, information, medicines and technologies, financing, and leadership and governance.
Health systems differ by country, so frameworks must be adapted to local law, resources and culture.
Governance is stewardship, accountability and regulation; financing involves revenue collection, pooling and purchasing.
Planning needs situation analysis, priorities, costing, implementation and review.
Leadership sets direction, management organises resources, and change management communicates, involves staff and monitors effects.

en.title: Health economics and financing
en.short: Scarcity, demand, market failure, insurance models, costs and cost-effectiveness in health.

sections.heading: Scarcity and demand
sections.text: Health economics studies how scarce resources are allocated. Scarcity means wants exceed resources, so every choice has an opportunity cost: the value of the best alternative forgone. Demand is the quantity of care people are willing and able to buy at a given price; need is what would benefit them. In health care, demand responds to price, income, time costs and quality, but emergency care is less price-sensitive. Supply is limited by staff, facilities and medicines. Clinicians also influence demand, which is supplier-induced demand.

sections.heading: Market failure and insurance
sections.text: Health markets fail for several reasons. Information asymmetry means patients cannot judge quality or need. Externalities arise when treatment protects others, as with vaccination. Public goods, such as disease surveillance, are non-excludable and non-rivalrous. Insurance faces adverse selection, where sicker people are more likely to enrol, and moral hazard, where cover changes behaviour. Insurance works by pooling risk: many people prepay into a fund so costs are shared. Prepayment protects against catastrophic costs.

sections.heading: Financing models
sections.text: Financing models include tax-funded national health services, social health insurance linked to contributions, private voluntary insurance, community-based health insurance and out-of-pocket payment. Tax and social insurance pool risk widely; out-of-pocket payment does not, and can cause financial hardship. A financing system is judged by revenue raising, pooling and purchasing. Purchasing means deciding which services to buy and from whom.

sections.heading: Costs and evaluation
sections.text: Costs are fixed, variable, average or marginal. Economic evaluation compares costs and outcomes. Cost-effectiveness analysis uses a natural outcome, such as cases detected; cost-utility analysis uses quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), where one year in perfect health equals 1. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) = (cost of new − cost of old) ÷ (effect of new − effect of old). Suppose new costs 10,000 units and gives 8 QALYs; old costs 4,000 and gives 6 QALYs. ICER = (10,000 − 4,000) ÷ (8 − 6) = 6,000 ÷ 2 = 3,000 units per QALY. Lower ICER means better value. Compare it with the local willingness-to-pay threshold, set nationally, not universally.

keyPoints: Scarcity creates opportunity cost: choosing one service forgoes another.
Demand is willingness and ability to pay; need is capacity to benefit.
Health markets fail through information asymmetry, externalities, public goods, adverse selection and moral hazard.
Insurance pools risk through prepayment; out-of-pocket payment does not pool risk.
ICER = (cost new − cost old) ÷ (effect new − effect old); lower ICER means better value.
Compare ICER with the country’s willingness-to-pay threshold, not a universal cut-off.

en.title: Public health programme planning and evaluation
en.short: Needs assessment, objectives, logic models, indicators and process, outcome and impact evaluation.

sections.heading: Needs and objectives
sections.text:
Planning begins with a needs assessment: a systematic review of the health problem, who is affected, existing services and gaps.

Define the problem precisely, because a vague problem produces vague action. Objectives state what will change, for whom, by how much and by when. Distinguish process objectives, about delivery and coverage, from outcome objectives, about behaviour or health. Good objectives are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

sections.heading: Logic models
sections.text:
A logic model, or programme theory, sets out the assumed chain: inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes and impact. Inputs are resources; activities are what the programme does; outputs are direct products, such as sessions held or people screened; outcomes are changes in knowledge, behaviour or health; impact is longer-term health change.

Evaluation questions follow from this chain. Was delivery as planned? Did outputs reach the intended group? Did outcomes change? Can impact be attributed? Test weak links rather than assuming them.

sections.heading: Indicators and errors
sections.text:
An implementation plan states who does what, where, when and with what resources, plus monitoring and risk plans.

Indicators are measures used to judge change. Process indicators describe delivery; output indicators describe direct products and coverage; outcome indicators describe short-term change; impact indicators describe health status. Avoid common errors: choosing an easy indicator unrelated to the objective; mixing numerator and denominator; changing definitions mid-programme; and treating a target as evidence. Record each indicator’s definition, source, frequency and denominator. Use a baseline and, where feasible, a comparison group.

sections.heading: Worked case
sections.text:
Case: a district screens adults for raised blood pressure. Baseline: 20,000 adults, 5,000 screened in a year = 25% coverage. After adding community clinics, 7,500 are screened = 37.5% coverage.

Clinics held is a process indicator; coverage is an output indicator; blood pressure control is an outcome indicator; strokes over years would be impact indicators. The rise in coverage does not prove impact, because other factors may act. Evaluation questions should match the logic model and available resources.

keyPoints: A needs assessment defines the problem, affected group, existing services and gaps before objectives are set.
Objectives should state the change, group, amount and time, and separate process from outcome.
A logic model links inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes and impact, and evaluation questions should follow that chain.
Process evaluation asks whether delivery happened as planned; outcome and impact evaluation ask whether change occurred and can be attributed.
Coverage = (people reached ÷ eligible population) × 100; record definitions, sources and denominators.
Avoid easy but irrelevant indicators, mixed denominators, changed definitions and treating targets as evidence.

en.title: Implementation science and scale-up
en.short: The evidence-to-practice gap, frameworks, fidelity, context, barriers and scale-up.

sections.heading: The evidence-to-practice gap
sections.text:
Implementation science studies methods to promote the systematic uptake of proven interventions into routine practice. It starts from a common problem: many effective programmes never reach the people who need them, or reach them weakened. This is the evidence-to-practice gap.

Implementation differs from programme evaluation. Evaluation asks whether an intervention worked and at what cost. Implementation research asks how and why it was, or was not, delivered as intended.

sections.heading: Frameworks and fidelity
sections.text:
Frameworks guide the work. Determinant frameworks list the factors that influence uptake. Process models describe stages, such as the Exploration, Preparation, Implementation, Sustainment framework. RE-AIM tracks Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation and Maintenance. Rogers’ diffusion of innovations explains how new practices spread through a social system.

Fidelity means delivering an intervention as designed: its core components, dose and quality of delivery. Adaptation means changing it to fit local needs. The usual guidance is to keep core functions and adapt the form. Too much adaptation loses effect; too little fails to fit.

sections.heading: Context and barriers
sections.text:
Context is the setting and conditions around delivery: policy, funding, staffing, culture, and the views of patients and staff. Barriers and facilitators are studied with mixed methods: interviews for meaning, surveys for spread, and observation or records for actual practice.

A case: a district plans to add a hypertension register to its clinics. Interviews show nurses expect extra paperwork with no staff. A survey shows only some clinics have working blood pressure machines. Both findings shape the plan before it starts.

sections.heading: Sustainability and scale-up
sections.text:
Sustainability is continued delivery after initial support ends. Scale-up is deliberate expansion to more sites or populations, often through policy. Scale-up is not replication: what works in a well-resourced pilot may fail elsewhere.

A worked example: a pilot in 8 clinics reaches 70 per cent of eligible patients. A district with 60 clinics aims for the same coverage. If 45 clinics adopt within a year, adoption is 45 ÷ 60 = 0.75, or 75 per cent. Coverage must be measured again, because adoption is not delivery.

keyPoints: Implementation science studies how proven interventions get into routine practice; the evidence-to-practice gap is the shortfall.
Implementation research asks how and why delivery happened; evaluation asks whether the intervention worked.
Frameworks such as determinant frameworks, process models and RE-AIM organise the questions.
Keep core functions and adapt the form: fidelity and adaptation must be balanced.
Study barriers and facilitators with mixed methods, and treat context as part of the intervention.
Scale-up is not replication; measure coverage again after adoption.

en.title: Health promotion and behaviour change
en.short: It covers principles, behaviour theories, settings, communication, mobilisation and policy for health promotion.

sections.heading: Promotion and prevention
sections.text: Health promotion is the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health. It acts on determinants through population and settings measures. Clinical prevention delivers services to individuals, such as screening or immunisation, in health services. They overlap, but promotion adds policy, environment, community and communication. Social theory explains how society shapes health; here you apply theory to design action.

sections.heading: Behaviour change theories
sections.text: Behaviour change theories explain why people act as they do and suggest what to change. The Health Belief Model uses perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits and barriers, plus cues and self-efficacy. The Theory of Planned Behaviour links attitudes, subjective norms and perceived behavioural control to intention. Social Cognitive Theory stresses self-efficacy, observational learning and reciprocal influence between person and environment. Stages of Change describes precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance, with relapse possible at any stage. COM-B links capability, opportunity and motivation to behaviour. Use theory to diagnose, not blame individuals.

sections.heading: Settings and action
sections.text: Settings-based approaches treat schools, workplaces, markets, health facilities and cities as whole systems, changing rules, physical space and culture, not only teaching individuals. Health communication uses formative research, audience segmentation, pretesting and trusted channels such as community radio. It should give practical, consistent messages and avoid fear without a clear action. Community mobilisation builds local leadership, participation and ownership through coalitions and community diagnosis. Policy action includes healthy public policy, fiscal measures, regulation and legislation, supported by advocacy and health in all policies.

sections.heading: Case in practice
sections.text: In a fictional district in northern Nigeria, Amina leads a team tackling child obesity. A survey shows few safe water points near schools and many sweet drinks sold at the market. Using COM-B, the team finds that children lack opportunity, not motivation. They work with head teachers on a school water policy, market leaders on vendor rules, and a radio station on short spots. The local government adds water points to its budget. Progress is measured by water availability and drink sales, not only by knowledge scores.

keyPoints: The Ottawa Charter (1986) defines health promotion as enabling people to increase control over and improve their health.
Clinical prevention serves individuals in health services; health promotion adds policy, environment, community and communication.
Behaviour change theories diagnose influences on behaviour and should not be used to blame individuals.
Settings-based approaches change rules, spaces and culture in schools, workplaces and cities, not only individual knowledge.
Effective health communication uses formative research, segmentation, pretesting and trusted channels.
Community mobilisation and healthy public policy shift power and environments, not just messages.

en.title: Environmental health and sanitation
en.short: Water, sanitation, air quality, waste, vectors, hazards, exposure assessment and climate risks.

sections.heading: Water, sanitation and hygiene
sections.text: Environmental health studies how physical, chemical and biological conditions around people affect health. Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) are core. Safe water means free from pathogens and harmful chemicals at the point of use. Sanitation means safe management of human excreta, including toilets and treatment. Hygiene means behaviours such as handwashing with soap. Population prevention includes protecting water sources, treating water, safe storage, sewerage or safe latrines, and handwashing facilities. Standards for water quality and sanitation differ by country; check the current national rules and WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Air, waste and vectors
sections.text: Air pollution harms health outdoors and indoors. Fine particles (PM2.5) and gases from traffic, industry and cooking smoke are key. Waste management covers household, industrial and health-care waste; hazardous waste needs separate handling. Vector control reduces mosquitoes, flies and rodents through drainage, safe storage, larviciding and bed nets. These measures work best as programmes, not single actions.

sections.heading: Hazards and exposure
sections.text: A hazard is something that can cause harm; risk is the chance and severity of harm. Exposure assessment estimates who contacts a hazard, by what route (inhalation, ingestion, skin), and for how long. Example: well water contains 0.05 mg/L arsenic and a 50 kg person drinks 2 L/day. Intake = 0.05 × 2 = 0.1 mg/day. Dose = 0.1 ÷ 50 = 0.002 mg/kg/day. Compare with the current national or WHO guideline; the WHO arsenic guideline is 0.01 mg/L, so this water exceeds it. Prevention: remove or dilute the hazard, protect people, and monitor.

sections.heading: Climate and prevention
sections.text: Climate change raises heat stress, floods, drought, water scarcity and vector-borne disease risks. Population prevention includes early warning, safe water and sanitation, vector surveillance, and climate-resilient infrastructure. Risk assessment combines hazard, exposure and vulnerability. Regulations vary, so use current national standards and WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Environmental health prevents population harm from water, air, waste, vectors, chemicals and climate.
Safe WASH needs source protection, treatment, safe excreta management and handwashing.
Air pollution and waste affect health; control needs programmes, not single actions.
Exposure assessment estimates route, amount and duration; intake = concentration × amount per day, and dose = intake ÷ body weight.
Risk combines hazard, exposure and vulnerability; compare findings with current national or WHO standards.
Climate adaptation includes early warning, resilient water and sanitation, and vector surveillance.

en.title: Occupational health and safety
en.short: Hazards, exposure assessment, occupational disease, surveillance and worker protection.

sections.heading: Hazards and exposure
sections.text:
Occupational health and safety protects workers from work-related illness and injury. A hazard is anything with potential to cause harm; risk is the chance and severity of that harm. Hazards are physical, chemical, biological, ergonomic and psychosocial. Exposure assessment identifies the agent, route (inhalation, skin, ingestion) and dose. For an 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA), multiply each concentration by its duration, add, then divide by 8.

Example: 20 parts per million (ppm) for 4 hours and 60 ppm for 4 hours gives (20×4 + 60×4) ÷ 8 = 40 ppm. Compare with the current occupational exposure limit (OEL) for that country.

sections.heading: Disease and injury
sections.text: Occupational diseases are caused or worsened by work. Examples include pneumoconiosis (dust-related lung disease) from mineral dust, occupational asthma, contact dermatitis, noise-induced hearing loss and infections such as hepatitis B in health workers. They often appear after years of exposure, so an exposure history is essential. Occupational injuries are acute events such as falls, machinery accidents and work-related road crashes. Both are preventable and should be recorded and investigated.

sections.heading: Surveillance and prevention
sections.text:
Surveillance has two arms. Workplace monitoring measures hazards, such as air sampling for dust or noise measurement with a sound level meter. Worker health surveillance checks for early signs of work-related disease. Reporting schemes for injuries and diseases reveal patterns and guide action.

Prevention follows a hierarchy: eliminate the hazard, substitute a safer material, use engineering controls such as ventilation or guards, then administrative controls such as rotation and training, and finally personal protective equipment (PPE). PPE is last because it depends on correct use. Worker health protection includes training, safe systems of work, health surveillance and return-to-work support.

sections.heading: Law and enforcement
sections.text: Occupational legislation, exposure limits and enforcement differ by country. National laws set duties on employers and workers, and labour inspectorates or regulators enforce them; examples include OSHA in the United States and the HSE in Great Britain. Compensation systems also vary. Check current national law and guidance, and WHO and ILO resources.

keyPoints: A hazard is a potential source of harm; risk combines the chance and severity of harm.
Exposure assessment measures the agent, route and dose; for an 8-hour TWA, TWA = Σ(concentration × hours) ÷ 8.
Occupational diseases often have long latency, so exposure histories are essential.
Prevention follows the hierarchy: eliminate, substitute, engineer, use administrative controls, then PPE last.
Surveillance covers workplace monitoring, worker health checks and reporting of injuries and diseases.
Occupational legislation, exposure limits and enforcement differ by country; check current national law and WHO/ILO guidance.

en.title: Communicable disease control
en.short: Transmission, surveillance, outbreak investigation, immunisation and control of TB, HIV, malaria and AMR.

sections.heading: Transmission and surveillance
sections.text:
Transmission dynamics explains how infection spreads between people, vectors or the environment. R0 is the average secondary cases one infectious case would cause in a fully susceptible population. The effective reproduction number, Reff, reflects immunity and control. For simple random mixing, the herd immunity threshold is roughly 1 − 1/R0.

Surveillance is the continuous collection, analysis and use of health data. Passive surveillance uses routine reports; active surveillance seeks cases; sentinel sites monitor selected groups. Clear case definitions and feedback matter. Follow current WHO and national guidance, including Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response.

sections.heading: Outbreak investigation
sections.text: An outbreak is more cases than expected in a place and time. Investigate promptly: verify the diagnosis and confirm an outbreak; define a case; find cases and build a line list; describe time, place and person; generate hypotheses; test them with epidemiologic and laboratory methods; apply control measures; communicate clearly. Control can begin before the cause is certain. A food-borne outbreak in a school needs case finding, stool and food sampling, kitchen inspection and hygiene measures.

sections.heading: Immunisation
sections.text: Immunisation protects individuals and populations. Active immunisation uses a vaccine to stimulate immune memory; passive immunisation gives ready-made antibodies for short-term protection. Routine schedules, catch-up and campaigns raise coverage. The cold chain keeps vaccines effective. Monitor coverage and vaccine-preventable disease, and report adverse events after immunisation. High coverage can produce herd protection, but the threshold depends on the pathogen and setting. Use the current national schedule and WHO guidance; schedules differ by country.

sections.heading: Major diseases and AMR
sections.text: Control combines case finding, prompt treatment, contact tracing, infection prevention and vector or environmental measures. Tuberculosis needs early diagnosis, complete treatment and contact investigation under national programmes. HIV control uses testing, treatment and combination prevention. Malaria control uses insecticide-treated nets, indoor spraying where appropriate, prompt diagnosis and treatment, and chemoprevention for groups at risk. Antimicrobial resistance is slowed by stewardship, infection control, surveillance and access to quality medicines. Always follow current national and WHO guidance, because guidance changes.

keyPoints: R0 is the average number of secondary cases one infectious case causes in a fully susceptible population; Reff reflects current immunity and control.
For simple random mixing, the herd immunity threshold is roughly 1 − 1/R0.
Surveillance is continuous collection, analysis and use of health data; case definitions and feedback are essential.
Outbreak investigation follows steps from verification and case definition to line listing, hypothesis testing, control and communication.
Immunisation works through active vaccine-induced immunity or passive antibodies; coverage, cold chain and adverse event reporting determine impact.
TB, HIV, malaria and antimicrobial resistance are controlled through combined national and WHO-guided measures, not a single intervention.

en.title: Noncommunicable diseases: prevention, risk factors and health system response
en.short: Population prevention, shared risk factors, surveillance and health system responses to major NCDs.

sections.heading: What NCDs are
sections.text: NCDs are chronic conditions not spread from person to person. The main groups are cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancers and chronic respiratory disease. They develop over years and are shaped by social, commercial and environmental conditions. Many are preventable, and prevention works at population level, not only in clinics.

sections.heading: Shared risk factors
sections.text: Shared risk factors explain much of the burden. Modifiable behavioural risks include tobacco use, harmful alcohol use, unhealthy diet and physical inactivity. Metabolic risks include raised blood pressure, overweight and obesity, raised blood glucose and abnormal blood lipids. Air pollution is an important environmental risk. Some cancers have infectious causes, such as human papillomavirus for cervical cancer and hepatitis B for liver cancer. Risks cluster, so population measures such as tobacco control, salt reduction and clean air policy can reduce several diseases at once.

sections.heading: Surveillance and policy
sections.text: Surveillance is the ongoing collection, analysis and use of health data. For NCDs it draws on vital registration, cancer registries, national surveys and risk factor surveys such as WHO STEPS. Surveillance shows which risks and diseases matter locally and whether programmes are working. Policy responses include the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control, alcohol control, salt and food reform, physical activity promotion, clean air measures, and vaccination against hepatitis B and human papillomavirus. Screening follows national policy, because eligibility and intervals differ by country.

sections.heading: Health system response
sections.text: Health system responses include integrating NCD prevention into primary health care, using team-based care, maintaining information systems and ensuring reliable medicines and diagnostics. Services should support risk assessment, referral, long-term follow-up and self-management, following current national guidelines. For example, Amina, a district health officer in Ghana, uses survey and clinic data to find that tobacco use and raised blood pressure are common. She adds brief advice, cessation referral, salt-reduction messages and blood pressure checks to primary care, then tracks coverage. Clinical treatment details are outside this summary; check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: The four main NCD groups share a small set of modifiable and metabolic risks.
Tobacco, harmful alcohol, unhealthy diet, inactivity and air pollution are key population risks.
Raised blood pressure, obesity and raised blood glucose often cluster with behavioural risks.
Population-wide policy can shift risk across the whole population and reduce several diseases at once.
Surveillance combines vital registration, registries, surveys and WHO STEPS to guide local action.
Health systems should integrate prevention, early detection, referral and follow-up into primary care, following current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Maternal, newborn and child health
en.short: The continuum of care, causes of maternal, newborn and child deaths, interventions and health system needs.

sections.heading: The continuum of care
sections.text: The continuum of care links services from pregnancy through birth, the postnatal period and childhood. It means care is connected across time and across levels: household and community, primary care, and referral hospitals. Antenatal care finds and manages risks such as anaemia and hypertension. Skilled birth attendance means care at birth by a trained professional. Postnatal care covers the mother and newborn in the first days and weeks, when many deaths occur. Child health services then continue promotion, prevention and treatment. The same woman and child should not be lost between separate programmes. Service packages and targets vary by country, so check current national guidance.

sections.heading: Causes and population interventions
sections.text: Major maternal causes include haemorrhage, hypertensive disorders such as pre-eclampsia, sepsis, obstructed labour and unsafe abortion. Newborn deaths are driven mainly by preterm birth, complications around birth and infections. Child deaths are concentrated in pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria and malnutrition, with neonatal causes important in the first month. Evidence-based population interventions include family planning, quality antenatal and postnatal care, skilled birth attendance, emergency obstetric and newborn care, immunisation, breastfeeding support, oral rehydration salts with zinc for diarrhoea, insecticide-treated nets and integrated management of childhood illness. Community health workers can promote care-seeking and follow-up. For example, a district team finds that newborn deaths cluster in the first week and adds postnatal home visits and a transport plan for referrals.

sections.heading: Health system requirements
sections.text: Delivering this continuum needs a trained and supported workforce, reliable supplies and medicines, functioning referral and transport, blood services, and good data. Financing must cover free or affordable care at the point of use, especially for poor families. Quality matters: respectful care, infection control and audit of deaths and near misses. Community engagement and women’s voice help services reach those most at risk. Countries set their own service packages, indicators and targets, and these change. Students should compare local plans with WHO guidance and current national policy rather than assume one package fits all.

keyPoints: The continuum of care links pregnancy, birth, postnatal and child services across household, primary and referral levels.
Major maternal causes include haemorrhage, hypertensive disorders, sepsis, obstructed labour and unsafe abortion.
Newborn deaths are driven mainly by preterm birth, complications around birth and infections; child deaths by pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria and malnutrition.

Evidence-based interventions include family planning, skilled birth attendance, emergency obstetric and newborn care, immunisation, breastfeeding support, oral rehydration salts with zinc and insecticide-treated nets.
Health systems need trained staff, supplies, referral and transport, blood, data, financing and respectful quality care.
Service packages, indicators and targets vary by country; check current national policy and WHO guidance.

en.title: Public health nutrition
en.short: Population nutrition: undernutrition, micronutrients, obesity, food security, assessment and policy.

sections.heading: Undernutrition and micronutrients
sections.text: Public health nutrition studies how food and nutrient intake affect populations, not just patients. Undernutrition includes stunting (low height for age), wasting (low weight for height) and underweight (low weight for age). It raises infection risk and slows development. Micronutrient deficiencies, sometimes called hidden hunger, occur when vitamins or minerals are too low even if energy intake is adequate. Common examples are iron deficiency anaemia, vitamin A deficiency and iodine deficiency disorders. Population assessment uses anthropometry (body measurements such as height and weight), biochemical tests and dietary data, interpreted against World Health Organization (WHO) growth standards or national cut-offs.

sections.heading: Obesity and food security
sections.text: Overweight and obesity mean excess body fat that harms health. In adults, BMI is weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared. For example, 70 kg and 1.60 m gives 70 ÷ (1.60 × 1.60) = 70 ÷ 2.56 = 27.3 kg/m², which is overweight on the WHO adult scale. BMI is a screening tool, not a diagnosis, and child or pregnancy cut-offs differ. Food security means reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food. Its four dimensions are availability, access, utilisation (how the body uses the food) and stability. Obesity and food insecurity can coexist, especially where cheap energy-dense food is abundant.

sections.heading: Assessment and fortification
sections.text: Dietary assessment estimates what people eat. A 24-hour recall asks about foods eaten yesterday; a food frequency questionnaire asks how often foods are eaten; food balance sheets describe national supply. Each has bias: recall depends on memory, and questionnaires need validation. Fortification adds micronutrients to widely eaten foods, such as iodised salt or vitamin A fortified oil. It is a population measure, not a prescription, and needs regulation, monitoring and quality control.

sections.heading: Nutrition policy
sections.text: Nutrition policy acts on the food environment. Examples include food labelling, controls on marketing to children, taxes on sugary drinks, school meal standards and support for breastfeeding. Policy should be evidence-based, monitored and adapted to local food systems. Countries differ in laws and programmes, so check current national guidance and WHO recommendations rather than assuming one model.

keyPoints: Undernutrition includes stunting, wasting and underweight; micronutrient deficiencies can occur even when energy intake is adequate.
BMI = weight in kg ÷ (height in m)²; it screens populations but does not diagnose individuals.
Food security has four dimensions: availability, access, utilisation and stability.
Dietary assessment methods include 24-hour recall, food frequency questionnaires and food balance sheets, each with limitations.
Fortification adds micronutrients to staple foods and requires regulation and monitoring.
Nutrition policy should target the food environment and be checked against current national and WHO guidance.

en.title: Global health and international cooperation
en.short: Burden of disease, actors and financing, SDGs, diplomacy, aid and cross-border threats.

sections.heading: Burden and actors
sections.text: Global health studies health problems that cross borders and the rules and resources used to address them. The global burden of disease measures lost health using the disability-adjusted life year (DALY): one DALY is one lost year of healthy life, from premature death or disability. The Global Burden of Disease study, coordinated by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, compares causes across countries, but estimates depend on data quality. Major actors include national governments, the World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF, the World Bank, the Global Fund (for AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria), Gavi (the Vaccine Alliance), bilateral agencies, foundations and NGOs.
