Financing comes from domestic budgets, out-of-pocket payments, insurance and development assistance for health. Who pays shapes what is treated.

sections.heading: Goals and diplomacy
sections.text: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are 17 goals adopted by UN member states in 2015. SDG 3 seeks good health and well-being, including universal health coverage (UHC): all people receive needed health services without financial hardship. Health diplomacy is negotiation between states and other actors over health rules, aid and shared threats. Examples include the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control and the International Health Regulations (IHR), which set obligations for outbreak reporting and response. Countries interpret targets differently: UHC may be measured by service coverage, financial protection or both, and priorities reflect local disease patterns and politics.

sections.heading: Aid, threats and power
sections.text: Aid can save lives, but it can also create dependence and fragment services. Vertical programmes target one disease; horizontal approaches strengthen whole systems. Principles such as country ownership and alignment matter. Cross-border threats include epidemics, antimicrobial resistance, migration and climate change. The IHR require countries to report public health events, but compliance depends on capacity and trust. Power and equity are central: high-income donors often set agendas, while low-income countries bear more disease and fewer resources. COVAX, set up during the COVID-19 pandemic to pool vaccine buying and share doses with poorer countries, showed both the promise and the limits of cooperation. In a fictional case, a West African country receives donor funding for HIV but lacks laboratory staff for outbreak detection; ministry and partners must balance both. Global targets are political compromises, so check current WHO and national guidance.

keyPoints: One DALY is one lost year of healthy life, combining premature death and disability.
Global health actors include governments, WHO, UNICEF, the World Bank, the Global Fund, Gavi, foundations and NGOs.
Health financing mixes domestic spending, out-of-pocket payments, insurance and development assistance.
SDG 3 includes universal health coverage, but countries measure and prioritise it differently.
Health diplomacy uses instruments such as the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control and the International Health Regulations.
Power shapes aid: donor priorities can override local ownership, so equity requires attention to who sets the agenda.

en.title: Health information systems and informatics
en.short: Health data sources, records, quality, privacy and use of information for decisions.

sections.heading: Data sources
sections.text: A health information system is the people, processes, data and technology that collect, store, analyse and share health information. Sources include routine facility and community reports, disease surveillance, surveys, censuses, civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS), administrative records and research. CRVS records births, deaths and causes of death; vital statistics are the counts and rates derived from them. Completeness varies, and deaths without medical certification weaken cause-of-death data. Household surveys such as the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) and Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS) give population-based estimates, including for people who do not use facilities. They are periodic and depend on recall. Routine health information systems (RHIS) show service use, not all illness.

sections.heading: Records and quality
sections.text: Electronic health records (EHRs) and electronic medical records (EMRs) store clinical data digitally. They can improve legibility, sharing and decision support, but poor design, downtime and weak security create risks. Data quality is judged by completeness, accuracy, timeliness, consistency and validity. Poor data mislead policy. Suppose a district’s malaria reports fall from 500 to 200 cases in a month. The health officer checks completeness and finds two high-burden clinics sent no report. The fall was a reporting gap, not a true decline. Acting on the raw total could move resources away from areas that need them. Good systems check data, give feedback to facilities and use information to plan and monitor services.

sections.heading: Privacy and digital health
sections.text: Privacy means protecting identifiable health information. Confidentiality, consent, access controls, encryption and anonymisation reduce harm, but data protection law differs by country, so follow current national rules. Digital health covers EHRs, mobile health, telehealth and linked data. It can speed reporting and reach distant communities, but needs electricity, connectivity, trained staff and interoperability, meaning systems can exchange and use data. Without governance, digital tools can widen inequity or expose data. Use information systems to ask whether services are accessible, effective and equitable, not only to count contacts. Check WHO and national digital health guidance.

keyPoints: A health information system links data collection, storage, analysis and use for decisions.
CRVS records births and deaths, surveys give population estimates, and routine systems show service contacts.
Data quality is judged by completeness, accuracy, timeliness, consistency and validity.
Electronic records can improve sharing and decision support but need security, reliable infrastructure and good design.
Incomplete or poor data can make policy makers underestimate need and misallocate resources.
Privacy and data protection law vary by country, so follow current national rules and WHO guidance.

en.title: Public health emergency preparedness and response
en.short: The disaster cycle, all-hazards planning, early warning, risk communication, coordination, recovery and the IHR.

sections.heading: Disaster cycle and planning
sections.text: A public health emergency threatens health beyond routine capacity. The disaster cycle describes mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery. Mitigation reduces risk before an event, such as safe water systems. Preparedness includes plans, stockpiles, trained staff and exercises. Response saves lives and limits spread. Recovery restores services and learns lessons. All-hazards planning builds one set of capacities for many hazards, not a separate plan for every disease or disaster. It allows hazard-specific detail where needed.

sections.heading: Early warning and communication
sections.text: Early warning uses surveillance to detect threats before they spread. Indicator-based surveillance counts cases against thresholds; event-based surveillance listens to rumours, clinics and media, then verifies them. An alert is not a response until it is assessed. Risk communication gives timely, clear, honest information about what is known, unknown and being done. It engages communities and counters misinformation. Trust matters more than perfect certainty.

sections.heading: Coordination and the IHR
sections.text: Response needs coordination: one incident management structure, clear roles, regular situation reports and links with sectors such as water, transport and security. The International Health Regulations (2005) are a legally binding WHO framework. States Parties must build core capacities to detect and respond, and notify WHO of events that may constitute a public health emergency of international concern (PHEIC). WHO convenes an Emergency Committee and the Director-General decides whether an event is a PHEIC. The IHR is one framework, not the whole of preparedness.

sections.heading: Response versus investigation
sections.text: Routine outbreak investigation confirms a diagnosis, describes person, place and time, and controls a known problem within normal services. Emergency response begins when the event exceeds routine capacity or needs national or international action. It adds incident command, surge staffing, multi-sector coordination, public communication and recovery planning. The two overlap. Case: in a fictional district, nurses report severe diarrhoea after a flood. The routine team finds contaminated water. Cases exceed district capacity, so an emergency operations centre opens, water trucking begins and daily risk messages are issued. Recovery repairs the supply and reviews the response.

keyPoints: The disaster cycle has mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery phases.
All-hazards planning builds common capacities for many hazards rather than a separate plan for each one.
Early warning combines surveillance, verification and timely risk communication.
Coordination needs an incident management structure, clear roles and regular situation reports.
The International Health Regulations (2005) require States Parties to build core capacities and notify WHO of events that may be a PHEIC.
Emergency response differs from routine outbreak investigation by adding surge, command and multi-sector action when routine capacity is exceeded.

en.title: Quality improvement and patient safety in health systems
en.short: Quality dimensions, measurement, improvement methods, safety, accreditation and learning from adverse events.

sections.heading: Quality dimensions
sections.text: Quality in health care is the degree to which services increase the chance of desired health outcomes and are consistent with current professional knowledge. Common dimensions are safety, effectiveness, patient-centredness, timeliness, efficiency and equity. Donabedian’s model links structure (resources and organisation), process (what is done) and outcome (what happens to patients). A service can have good outcomes despite weak processes, so all three are assessed.

sections.heading: Measuring quality
sections.text: Measurement uses indicators: defined counts or rates compared with a standard. Clinical audit compares care with agreed criteria and feeds results back. Run charts and statistical process control distinguish random variation from real change. Example: a clinic audits hand hygiene over 100 observed opportunities. Baseline compliance is 40/100 = 40%. After a change it is 55/100 = 55%. The absolute gain is 15 percentage points; relative gain is 15/40 = 37.5%. The team checks whether the shift is sustained.

sections.heading: Improvement methods
sections.text: Improvement methods turn measurement into action. The Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle tests a small change, studies the result and adapts it. Lean removes waste, and Six Sigma reduces variation. Multidisciplinary teams, clear aims and repeated cycles matter more than one-off campaigns. Changes should be tested locally before spread, because context affects results.

sections.heading: Safety and learning
sections.text: Patient safety is the prevention of avoidable harm from care. An adverse event is harm caused by care, not by the disease. A near miss is an event that could have harmed someone but did not. Safety science separates active failures, such as a slip by a worker, from latent conditions, such as poor staffing or unclear procedures. The Swiss cheese model shows how weaknesses in several defences line up. Just culture distinguishes human error, at-risk behaviour and reckless conduct, so reporting is encouraged without removing accountability. Incident reports, root cause analysis and mortality reviews should lead to system changes. Accreditation is external review against standards; it can prompt improvement but does not prove safety.

keyPoints: Quality has six common dimensions: safety, effectiveness, patient-centredness, timeliness, efficiency and equity.
Donabedian’s structure-process-outcome model guides assessment.
Compliance rate = compliant observations ÷ total observations × 100; absolute change is in percentage points, and relative change = absolute change ÷ baseline × 100.
PDSA cycles test small changes and study results before spread.
Patient safety focuses on systems and latent conditions, not individual blame.
Incident reporting, root cause analysis and accreditation support learning, but accreditation alone does not prove safety.
